name: Liver / organ meats (beef liver)

lead: Beef liver is rich in preformed vitamin A, vitamin B12, riboflavin, copper and iron, and in looksmaxxing and ancestral-diet circles it is eaten as a whole-food alternative to multivitamins for skin, energy and general vitality.

The chain is that nutrients concentrated in liver support skin, hair and energy. The nutrient content is well documented in reference sources; no published human trial has tested liver for skin, facial appearance or attractiveness.

paras: People cook it as slices or pan-fried pieces, mix it into ground beef, or take it frozen in small pieces. Forum members disagree about eating it raw, frozen or cooked, and many eat it as an occasional food rather than daily.

A single serving of liver can exceed the adult tolerable upper intake level of 3,000 micrograms per day of preformed vitamin A. Excess preformed vitamin A is associated with headaches, liver damage, bone effects and, in pregnancy, harm to the fetus, and health agencies advise limits, especially in pregnancy. Raw liver carries the food-safety concerns of any raw meat.

chain: Vitamin A, B12 and iron intake
angle.text: Forum users eat beef liver for its vitamin A, B12 and iron, expecting healthier skin and more vitality. Its nutrient content is well documented; trials on appearance have not been done.

lead: Liver is the organ most often meant by the term organ meats or offal in looksmaxxing and ancestral-diet communities. Beef liver in particular is promoted online as one of the most nutrient-dense foods available, rich in preformed vitamin A, vitamin B12, riboflavin, copper and iron, and is described by some forum users as nature's multivitamin [1][2]. People who eat it for their looks usually cite skin, hair, energy and training capacity: vitamin A is involved in the maintenance of skin and mucosal barriers, and B12 and iron are involved in red blood cell production and energy metabolism [3][2].

Eating liver became a visible part of fitness and appearance culture through the 'ancestral lifestyle' persona of Brian Johnson, known as the Liver King, who went viral in 2021 for eating raw organs and meat, and through carnivore and animal-based diet influencers such as Paul Saladino, who co-owns an organ-supplement company with Johnson [4][5]. Offal is an old food rather than a new one, eaten in cuisines from Britain and Ireland to Lebanon, Japan and Peru, and recent reporting links a rise in Irish offal consumption partly to fitness influencers [6].

Reference sources confirm that liver is unusually nutrient-dense and that its preformed vitamin A content is high enough that one slice of beef liver can exceed the adult tolerable upper intake level of 3,000 micrograms per day [2][7]. The same sources document vitamin A poisoning from liver, historically from polar bear, seal and husky livers, and advise caution in pregnancy [2][7][3]. No published trial has tested whether eating liver changes skin quality, facial appearance or attractiveness; the appearance claims on forums rest on the food's nutrient profile and on personal reports.

paras: Liver is eaten in cuisines around the world and sits within the broader category of offal or organ meats [2][6]. It can be baked, boiled, fried, stir-fried, made into pâtés and sausages such as liverwurst, or eaten raw in dishes such as Lebanese asbeh nayeh and liver sashimi [2]. Regional dishes include liver and onions in Britain, skilpadjies in South Africa, burbot liver in Finland and cod liver served with potatoes in Russia [2].

The word offal derives from Germanic roots referring to what falls off in butchering. Organ meats were historically a food of poorer households, for example as the 'umble pie' of medieval England and in 18th and 19th century Ireland, where butchers exporting offcuts provoked rioting in Dublin in the late 18th century [6]. Liver also appears early in the record, with deer liver mentioned as a household dish in the Man'yoshu, compiled around the 7th to 8th century [6]. Ireland exported 134 million euros of offal in 2022, and offal consumption there has been reported to rise partly because of awareness of its nutritional value promoted by fitness influencers [6].

Liver is a source of protein and of several micronutrients in high concentration. Wikipedia's table for raw pork liver lists about 6,500 micrograms of vitamin A, 26 micrograms of vitamin B12, 3 mg of riboflavin, 15 mg of niacin and 23 mg of iron per 100 g, and notes that nutrient content varies among species [2]. Beef liver is reported at between about 4,970 and 21,145 micrograms of retinol activity equivalents per 100 g, compared with about 957 for sweet potato and 843 for carrot, whose vitamin A comes as carotenoids [3]. A looksmax.org guide promoting beef liver lists vitamin A, B12 and copper per 100 g and argues that these concentrations make liver superior to a multivitamin [1].

Liver's B12 content is noted to have helped lead to the discovery of that vitamin [2]. The US recommended dietary allowance for vitamin A is 900 micrograms RAE per day for adult men and 700 for adult women, with 770 in pregnancy and 1,300 during lactation [3].

Vitamin A in the form of retinal is part of the visual pigment rhodopsin, and retinoic acid supports skin and mucosal barriers, including by promoting antimicrobial peptides. Deficiency is common in parts of Sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia and is linked to weaker infection resistance [3]. Retinoid drugs derived from the same family, such as topical tretinoin and oral isotretinoin, normalise follicle keratinisation and reduce sebum production in acne [3]. Proponents of liver draw on this biology to argue that dietary vitamin A supports clearer skin; no trial has tested liver for that outcome.

Hypervitaminosis A results from excess preformed vitamin A (retinol and retinyl esters), not from carotenoids such as beta-carotene, which can cause only a harmless orange skin discoloration. Liver is a major dietary source [7]. The tolerable upper intake level for adults aged 19 to 70 is 3,000 micrograms per day, and a single 68 g slice of beef liver is cited as containing about 6,410 micrograms [2][7]. The body's liver holds 80 to 90 percent of its vitamin A reserves [7].

Reported symptoms of vitamin A excess include headache, nausea, dizziness, dry and peeling skin, itching, hair loss, cracked lips and increased sun sensitivity. Serious effects include liver damage, high blood calcium and raised pressure within the skull [7]. Retinoic acid is reported to suppress bone-forming cells and promote bone resorption, with bone loss and fractures described in the literature [7]. Retinol intake above 4,500 micrograms per day in pregnancy has been associated with a higher birth-defect risk, and Wikipedia states that excess vitamin A can harm babies whose mothers consumed too much [2][3]. Treatment is stopping the high intake, after which most people recover fully [7].

Historical vitamin A poisonings from the livers of polar bears, walruses, bearded seals and huskies are documented, including a 1597 account by Gerrit de Veer and the 1913 illness and death of Xavier Mertz on Douglas Mawson's Antarctic expedition, although the husky-liver explanation has been contested since 2005 [2][7]. Other species carry other hazards: Nunavut advised pregnant women in 2012 to limit ringed seal liver because of mercury [2]. Cod liver oil is another concentrated source, with about 4,080 micrograms of vitamin A per tablespoon [7]. Looksmax.org users also discuss cod liver, comparing its vitamin A and D content with fish [8].

Whether to eat liver raw is one of the most argued questions in the community. The ancestral-lifestyle movement popularised raw consumption, and some looksmax.org posters insist liver must be raw and unfrozen, while others cook it, freeze it or find it unpalatable raw [1][6][9]. Posters on T Nation, a bodybuilding forum, report pan-frying beef, lamb and chicken liver in oil and salt, pressure-cooking it, and mixing it into ground-meat dishes to mask the flavour [10][11].

Raw liver is eaten in some cuisines [2]. Food-safety authorities generally describe raw meat as carrying bacterial and parasitic risks; one T Nation poster joked about the chance of salmonella from undercooked liver [12]. Looksmax.org threads include posts from members asking how much liver is too much, with vitamin A toxicity the recurring worry [13].

sections.h: Liver King and the ancestral movement
paras: Brian Michael Johnson, born in 1978 in Puerto Rico and trained in biochemistry at Texas Tech University, became known as the Liver King after going viral in 2021 with an 'ancestral lifestyle' built on nine ancestral tenets, including eating large amounts of raw organs and meat, especially liver [4]. He and his wife Barbara had sold fitness supplements online since 2015 [4].

In late 2022, leaked emails indicated he spent more than 11,000 dollars a month on anabolic steroids, after years of attributing his physique to lifestyle alone. He then apologised in a video, admitting a weekly testosterone dose and saying he had misled viewers about his 'pharmacological intervention' [4]. Followers filed a 25 million dollar lawsuit in December 2022 that was later discontinued [4]. Medical professionals had criticised his diet as high in saturated fat and his claims as misleading [4]. A Netflix documentary, Untold: The Liver King, appeared in 2025, and the Guardian's reviewer called it witty [4]. Johnson later denounced the carnivore diet in the film [4].

Carnivore diets have precedents in 19th century writers and physicians, and in 2018 the former orthopaedic surgeon Shawn Baker popularised the diet on social media; later variants added organ meats, fruit, honey and raw dairy [14]. Paul Saladino, an American psychiatrist born in 1977, advocated a strict meat-only diet in his 2020 book The Carnivore Code, then reported sleep problems, palpitations, cramps and lower testosterone on the strict version and added carbohydrates; he promotes organ meats and co-owns Heart & Soil, an Austin company selling encapsulated organ supplements, with Johnson [5].

Saladino has been criticised by science communicators such as Joe Schwarcz, and Wikipedia describes some of his claims as pseudoscientific; he has been involved in controversies over raw milk, including a 2023 Erewhon smoothie containing beef organs and raw milk [5]. Nutrition bodies such as the British Dietetic Association describe carnivore diets as fad diets and note risks including raised LDL cholesterol, low fibre and possible nutrient gaps [14]. Proponents counter that organ meats supply vitamins that muscle meat alone does not, and Wikipedia notes that organs are a major part of traditional Inuit diets [14].

On looksmax.org, beef liver is the subject of long guides that present it as the most nutrient-dense whole food, with sections on sourcing, preparation, comparison with multivitamins and special cases such as iron deficiency and cognition [1]. Other threads cover how to cook it, how to make it palatable and goat versus beef liver [6][15][16][9]. Capsules, sold as a way around the taste, are discussed alongside fresh liver [5].

On T Nation, lifters mention liver as a cheap food: one poster found organ meats at around 2.50 dollars per pound in a supermarket and tried beef liver, heart, tongue and tripe [17]. Users commonly report that taste is the main barrier, and some say grass-fed liver tastes milder [15]. The claims centre on skin clarity, energy, hair and testosterone-adjacent vitality, none of which has been tested specifically for liver in published trials.

No studies found. No published human trial has tested liver or organ-meat consumption for skin condition, facial appearance or attractiveness. The nutritional composition of liver and the effects of excess vitamin A are described in reference sources [2][7][3], but these are not studies of appearance outcomes. Large trials of high-dose retinol or beta-carotene supplements in smokers (ATBC and CARET) found increased lung cancer incidence, a finding about supplements rather than liver as a food [3].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org and T Nation, beef liver is promoted as a dense whole-food supplement for skin and vitality, and debate centres on raw versus cooked, taste and how much vitamin A is too much [1][6][15][10][13].
